title: Walking out to greet Shabbat
hook: the Safed mystics walk into the fields on Friday to meet Shabbat

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Ari, Isaac Luria, and the sparks waiting to be lifted. Your line was the lion. What small thing did you do with full attention? Today, the Ari's town on a Friday afternoon. Day nine hundred fifty-five.

Friday, late afternoon, on the edge of Tzfat. The cooking is done. The lamps are ready. And instead of waiting indoors, a group of men walk out of town, down the slope, into the fields. They face west, toward the setting sun, and begin to sing. They are not going anywhere. They are going out to meet someone. Tradition says the mystics of Tzfat did this week after week, as if the guest they were greeting were coming up the road. Today, walking out to greet Shabbat.
screen: `FRIDAY, LATE AFTERNOON.` → `OUT INTO THE FIELDS.` → `FACING THE SETTING SUN.`

segments.voice: The idea is older than Tzfat. The Talmud tells of two sages and their Friday habits. Rabbi Hanina would wrap himself in his cloak as the sun went down and say: come, let us go out to greet Shabbat the queen. Rabbi Yannai would put on his Shabbat clothes and say: come, O bride, come, O bride. Shabbat, in their words, is not just a day that arrives. She is someone you go out to meet. The mystics of Tzfat took those words literally and walked into the fields. Out of that circle came a poem, Lecha Dodi, written by Shlomo Halevi Alkabetz. Its refrain says, in Hebrew, lecha dodi likrat kallah: come, my beloved, to meet the bride. Look closely at the Hebrew: the first letters of its opening verses spell out the poet's name. The Friday evening psalms that welcome Shabbat in the synagogue, called Kabbalat Shabbat, grew from this same setting, and they lead into the psalm the Bible titles for the day. It begins: "A Psalm, a Song. For the sabbath day." Today the fields have mostly turned into a doorway. When the last verse of Lecha Dodi is sung, congregations often turn around to face the synagogue door and bow, as though the bride were walking in. It's a small movement. But it keeps the old walk alive: Shabbat is still greeted, not just noticed.
screen: `HANINA AND YANNAI GO OUT TO MEET HER.` · `THE MYSTICS WALK INTO THE FIELDS.` · `LECHA DODI: COME, MY BELOVED.` · then, large: `TURNING TO THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: greet Shabbat outdoors. If you can, step outside, or stand at a window that faces west. If it's not Friday, greet the evening instead, or simply the next rest you'll have. Let the light on the buildings and the sky be what you watch. Notice the change in it, slow and certain. Instead of waiting for rest to find you, turn toward it. If you pray, you can whisper the old words: come, O bride. The bell holds the time.
Walking out to greet Shabbat. Going out to meet the day of rest like a bride or a queen, as the Talmud's sages did and the mystics of Tzfat did in the fields. Today's word.
screen: `WALKING OUT TO GREET SHABBAT — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: walk out to meet her. Today, when your next rest comes, go to meet it: step outside, stand up, turn toward it, instead of letting it slip in unnoticed. Day nine hundred fifty-five.

howItsDone: On Friday evening, Jewish congregations sing Kabbalat Shabbat, including Lecha Dodi, and at its last verse the congregation often turns to face the door to welcome Shabbat as a bride.
